summary.text: 面 is a picture of a face, with an eye enclosed by an outline. It commonly means ‘face’ and also has recorded uses for ‘surface’ and ‘side’. In simplified Chinese, 面 also writes the flour and noodle word written 麵 in traditional Chinese; that is a separate word history.

formation.text: Pictographic: the oracle graph is interpreted as an enclosing face outline with an eye inside. The Shuowen account also describes it as shaped like a human face and derived from 𦣻. These are two accounts of the graph; the evidence does not establish 𦣻 as a separate component of 面.

components.text: The whole graph—an enclosing outline with an eye—depicts a face. It is best treated as one picture rather than split into modern components; the relation to 𦣻 in the Shuowen account does not establish a distinct component here.

history.text: An oracle form is analyzed as an outline enclosing an eye. 面 itself is reported unattested in bronze inscriptions. A Chu-slip form is said to have an enclosure altered toward 臼; these reports do not provide a complete sequence of graphic stages.
The Shuowen account derives 面 from 𦣻 and describes it as shaped like a human face. 靣 is recorded as a variant, with no established ancestry linking it to 面.

For the flour and noodle word, simplified Chinese uses 面 where traditional Chinese uses 麵. The related graph 麪 is recorded as an earlier spelling, analyzed with 麥 for meaning and 丏 for sound. The precise transition to 麵 is unresolved, and this spelling relationship does not show that the face word 面 gave rise to the food word.

uncertainties.text: The individual oracle inscriptions and their dates were not verified; the face reading is a modern analysis of the graph. The report that 面 is unattested in bronze inscriptions does not specify the limits of the surveyed corpus.
The dates and semantic links among the recorded uses ‘face toward’, ‘surface’, ‘side’ and ‘dimension’ remain unresolved.
The evidence does not establish the exact chronology of 麪 and 麵, separate earliest attestations for flour and noodles, or phonetic borrowing of the food word from the face word.

senses.period: oracle-bone script period; individual attestations undated
senses.text: The oracle graph is interpreted as depicting a face, while the Shuowen gloss describes the area before the face. This is the earliest supported sense here; the individual inscriptions were not dated.

senses.period: Chu-slip text cited by a modern database; date not supplied
senses.text: 面 is reported with the sense ‘face toward’ in a Chu-slip text.
Dictionary records list ‘surface’, ‘side’ and ‘dimension’. Their dates and connections to the face and facing senses are unresolved.

senses.gloss: flour, dough, noodles (written 面 in simplified Chinese for 麵)
senses.text: In simplified Chinese, 面 writes the flour and noodle word for which traditional Chinese uses 麵. This is a writing substitution; the evidence does not establish semantic development from ‘face’ or borrowing based on sound.

developments.text: The facing use is compatible with an extension from ‘face’, but its historical development is not established.

limitations.text: Dates and links among the facing, surface, side and dimension uses remain unresolved.
The relationship between 面 and 麵 as spellings is supported, but its exact chronology and any sound-based borrowing from the face word are not established.

The face outline enclosing an eye is supported as an analysis of 面’s oracle form, but neither supplied candidate image was successfully fetched for visual verification. With no inspectable glyph image, there is no candidate to select.

relationships.text: In simplified Chinese, 面 is the standardized counterpart of traditional 麵 in the flour and noodle word. This whole-character writing relationship does not make 麵 an internal component of 面 or establish borrowing from the face word.

overview.text: 面 pictures a face, with an eye enclosed by an outline. It commonly means ‘face’; simplified Chinese also uses it to write the separate flour and noodle word written 麵 in traditional Chinese.

components.text: Read the outline and eye together as one picture of a face, rather than as separate modern components.
